segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: My grandfather, Melvin, ran a hardware store in Baltimore that also sold model trains. And he had a huge-- and I mean huge-- train set in the basement of his house on Pimlico Road that I loved. This thing was vast, with tunnels and bridges and towns and streetlights that lit. And the train engines puff smoke as they scooted around the track on this big, wooden platform in the basement in the middle of all this epic amount of clutter and junk and his tools and, for some reason, a mimeograph machine.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And in the corner of the basement was the filthiest toilet I had ever seen-- like, frighteningly dirty to me as a little suburban kid. The whole basement was a chamber of chaos, and it was the most unsettlingly-chaotic thing in it. But that is not the story I'm here to tell. The story I'm here to tell is about Melvin and one of his sisters.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Uncle Bennett?

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: Yes, you got it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: To be sure I was getting the facts absolutely right on this thing, I called the last person in the family who might remember it, my Uncle Bennett. He was at home.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [PHONE RINGS]

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: Wait a minute. Hold on for one second.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah, well do.

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: Yeah, yeah. Hello? Hello? Yeah, Renee?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Renee is Bennett's girlfriend. They live together.

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: That was Renee. She wasn't sure if I was home.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Ah.

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: All right, anyway--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, wait. Is she in the house and she called you?

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I guess you're getting this-- these are older people who do not want to be bothered to cross the house or yell from room to room. Anyway, the story-- the story that I'm here to tell about my grandfather, Melvin, and his brothers and sisters.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Let me just give you the family geography here. He's one of four kids. And for the purposes of this particular story, you should imagine them in two competing teams. There are the two older kids, Melvin and Dorothy, and the two younger kids, Ray and Calvin.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, Melvin and Dorothy, Ray and Calvin. It's 1964, and their mom dies. The four kids are all in their 40s and 50s at this point. And then just after she died--

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: What happened was, Ray came up from Florida. And Calvin and Ray started taking things out of the house-- the silver tea service I remember that she had in the dining room. Whatever she had of value, they took.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And there was china, right? Like, the thing that I had always heard is that there was china and silverware.

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: Yeah, china, silverware, things like that. They just came in like hordes of locusts. And my father got nothing. And Dorothy apparently allegedly got nothing.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Again, the two older kids-- Melvin and Dorothy. The younger kids, Calvin and Ray, took all the good stuff.

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: And then my father was really upset about it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah. And Dorothy too, right?

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: Yeah, mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This, Bennett explained to me, was apparently typical behavior for Ray.

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: Ray was always-- like, when she was growing up, they used to say that at dinner, she would take the biggest piece of meat.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah, yeah. And then the way I remember it is that she takes the stuff, they fight about it, and they never spoke to Ray again.

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Didn't talk to her, didn't talk about her.

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: No, it was just too aggravating, you know?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Calvin, meanwhile-- Ray's partner in this family heist-- Calvin was a baby in the family, 13 years younger than the next-oldest kid. And the way that I always heard it, nobody held this against Calvin because everybody knew that Ray could just push him around and get him to do whatever she wanted.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So Calvin was around. I remember Calvin clowning around, doing little magic tricks for me at charity crab feasts that Dorothy used to organize all through my childhood.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But not Ray. It really was like Ray never existed, was never spoken about, off in Florida. I and my sisters met her only one time. Bennett, her own nephew-- Bennett only met her once on a trip to Miami after he was married.

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: And I called Ray. And she and Uncle Irvin came up, picked us up, and took us to Wolfie's-- [COUGH] pardon me-- which is a deli restaurant.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: That was the only contact I ever had with her my whole life.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then I remember when Melvin died, Ray not coming to his funeral.

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: No, of course not.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I remember being so stunned by that, that a person could be in such a fight with their own sibling that they wouldn't show up at their funeral.

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: Oh, it happens all the time, Ira. And it's usually over money.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I think this story really got to me when I was a kid, and I first heard it because it was the very first glimpse I had at the idea that you can destroy things completely-- like, totally wreck them beyond repair-- with somebody you know so well. I mean, I guess I'm lucky that I lived in a family where something like this would be so rare. But still, for me, personally, that has been a hard lesson to hold on to.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When I was married and things were going badly and we were in counseling and trying to patch it together for so many years-- like, more years than I want to admit here on the radio-- and I think part of it was because I just had this feeling, like, we are not people who get divorced. Like, we are bigger than that somehow. My mom was a marriage therapist. I just couldn't accept-- I think we both couldn't accept-- that we had just broken things between us so badly that there was no coming back from it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I just didn't want to admit that-- which brings me to Humpty Dumpty. I didn't know this, but some of my coworkers with little kids at home were talking about how unsettling Humpty Dumpty is to some of those kids. Laura said that at the doctor's office, there's a poster. And their two-year-old saw it and after that was like, someone can break and not go back together? And then remembered it when they went back to that office a year later.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Zoe's son, Max, is two and a half.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: I want to tell him to go back together.

segments.speaker: Zoe
segments.text: You want it to go back together?

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Yeah, to fix it.

segments.speaker: Zoe
segments.text: You want to fix Humpty Dumpty?

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Yeah. I cannot do it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We posted a thing on social media about this and got a ton of responses from parents whose kids were terrified of Humpty Dumpty. One said her preschooler couldn't stand to see her crack eggs in the kitchen because it reminded her of the nursery rhyme. Another said her two-year-old spent weeks asking if he could recreate the story with an egg from the fridge, which they did-- like, a few times-- puzzling over the impossibility of putting an egg back together once it's cracked.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A few people wrote to talk about how it messed them up as kids to picture Humpty Dumpty left there in pieces on the side of the road, sad look on his face. A woman named Isabella wrote, "I wondered if he had to exist conscious in his cracked state forever or if he would slowly die. Because he seemed to be still alive after he had cracked."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's something about that image of someone broken so badly that nothing can fix it, that things can go so wrong, the finality of that-- before you understand all the bad things that can happen in the world, how things come apart and people you love can die and you will die, before you get to any of the entropic, messy chaos of our world with its blackened toilets and its long-ago trashed model trains, you get this glimpse, this fat, cartoon, overdressed egg man smashed to tiny bits of shell and goo.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our program, people who hit a moment when things shatter apart-- now they make sense of it and not go to pieces themselves. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, Toy R Us. Sometimes there's a really specific moment when things fall apart, and you know exactly what the moment was, but you were left with no idea how or why it happened or-- more important-- how to put the thing back together. David Kestenbaum found a family that happened to, a father and son, years ago. And the son has thought about it ever since.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The son in this story, his name is Peter Ocko. And I don't usually love hearing people's dreams, but this is how our interview started.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: Can I tell you my dream last night?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Yes. Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: Because you know I've been sort of worrying about this-- I dreamt that I pulled into a store, ran inside to pick something up. And when I came outside, there was a guy standing there, and he had disassembled my entire car. And the pieces were just all over the parking lot. And I was like what did you do to my car? Why did you take it apart? And he goes, it was broken. We needed to fix it. And then I woke up. And I was like, OK. I'm the car, and you're the guy.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I'm happy to be the guy. Let's take the car apart. The whole story starts here. When Peter was a kid, his dad got a kind of dream job. This was in the late '70s.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: When I was 11, he got a job at the Milton Bradley Company.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Like the toy company.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: Yeah, the toy company-- as a toy inventor.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Oh my god.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: Yeah. Well, that's what I thought too. I was in sixth grade. And this was like, super street cred to go in and say, my dad works at Milton Bradley. Because they were a big deal back then. But they were a big deal for 100 years.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: In fact, my dad moved into his cubicle. And he was next to the guy who claimed to have invented Chutes and Ladders. So [LAUGHS] I don't think that's true, but the guy was old enough that it's possible.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The job was exciting for Peter's dad too. His dad had always been searching for a way to be successful. And success was the thing he imagined happening all at once. He saw himself as an inventor. And if he just had the right idea, the world would notice. His ship would come in. He actually read a lot of books about ships and captains.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Anyway, his previous attempt at conquering the world had not gone so well. He'd created these kind of cardboard models of famous landmarks that he tried to sell as kits.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: My mom and I and him-- I was an only child. And the three of us would go out to the garage with hairdryers and kind of shrink wrap these cardboard model kits and put them in UPS boxes. And that was our life for a few years. And then it just died. It just died. And so he was struggling because he saw himself as an idea guy. And so when he got the chance to go to Milton Bradley and be a game designer or a toy designer, I think he was super excited.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The one bad thing about the job was that Milton Bradley was 90 miles from where they lived in Massachusetts. So his dad would just work there the whole week, only come home on the weekends.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: I was in sixth grade. I hated it. I hated seeing him leave on a Sunday and then return the following week. And it was a long week, and I really missed him. So Fridays, when he pulled into the driveway, I was ecstatic. I just was so happy to see him. And he'd always come home with a box of stuff.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And the stuff in that box, it was kind of magical. This was 1977. And in that box were circuit boards and wires. Milton Bradley was making some of the first electronic games. Their big hit was Simon-- basically, an electronic version of Simon Says-- a kind of chunky Frisbee-shaped thing with four big buttons-- red, blue, green, yellow-- that would light up.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And it made these kind of square wave tones that were really distinctive.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: [TWO NOTES PLAY]

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It would play a sequence. You'd have to remember it and play it back.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [NOTE SEQUENCE PLAYS]

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [NOTE SEQUENCE PLAYS BACK]

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [NOTE SEQUENCE PLAYS]

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [NOTE SEQUENCE PLAYS BACK]

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: OK. Even back then, it was a little boring. I'll be honest. I don't think there were any parents saying, like, I can't get my kid off the Simon. But it did feel like you were holding some object from the future, just to press the buttons and hear these kinds of sounds for the first time. Peter and his dad would sit around in this sort of attic room at this big table and just mess around with this stuff.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: Opening the toys up for me and seeing the circuit board and understanding that this little circuit board was playing the game of Simon-- I would get in there with a screwdriver, pull it out, and then start playing around with it and changing the resistor here or there. You could make it speed up, and suddenly, it was generating electronic music at high speed and flashing lights. It just felt halfway between technology and magic, you know? And I think, for both of us, that was super exciting, you know.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: They'd build little electronic kits together, which could get kind of tense. His dad liked to follow instructions-- Peter, not so much. They'd share little discoveries with each other, like when Peter realized you could take the spring from a ballpoint pen, put it across the terminals of a 9-volt battery and the electricity flowing through it would make it glow, like the filament in a light bulb.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: But more than anything, it was a way to spend time together. Week after week, when his dad would come home, this was their routine. They'd go up to the third floor and just be together, sitting side by side at this big drafting table. And then one day, as Peter thinks he remembers it, a kind of remarkable thing happened in that room, something that changed their lives. It was just Peter there that day in the workshop.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: What I remember is he had gone back to work on a Monday morning and left behind a box of stuff. And in that box was a bunch of circuit boards for different things, including a Simon circuit board. And I remember pulling it out and connecting it up to some batteries and just tinkering around with it, playing around with it.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And then I remember just looking at the lights and thinking, like, well, let me unsolder the lights and see if a motor will work there. Because we had these little hobby motors laying around. So I took off the four lights, and then I connected two motors to where two of the lights had been and tried it again. And the motor spun. When the lights would have lit up, the motor spun. And I was like, that's cool.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: In his memory, he then had another idea. I wonder if you could use those motors to make the wheels turn on a little car. Then the Simon board would be controlling a car. That would be neat.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: There was a mode in the Simon game where you could tell it which lights you wanted. You could program the pattern yourself. So I was like, well, you could program left motor, right motor. And so it's like a programmable car.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: A programmable car. You could punch some buttons on it, tell it you wanted it to drive forward, turn right, drive some more, turn left. Then it would go and do it.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: My dad came back on the following Friday, and I was excited to show him this little thing I'd built. And he'd took a look at it. It wasn't like the symphony started playing. He's like, that's really cool. That's a good idea. And I was like, cool. You think I have a good idea. That's awesome.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: His dad brought the idea into work. And Milton Bradley started to develop it as an actual toy with Peter's dad leading the team. His dad would update him when he got home. Like, our little thing is still moving forward. And as it got further along, he'd bring home these kind of handmade prototypes of it. The toy that was taking form was sort of a tank, dump truck kind of thing. You could program it to carry something to a place and drop it off, all on its own.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: I remember one problem they had was they couldn't get the tank to go perfectly straight. I remember my dad having this eureka moment one day and being like, oh. And he put two magnets opposing each other on the end of the shaft that wasn't on the wheel so that the motors lined up with these magnets and the magnets grabbed each other without actually touching and kept the motors moving at exactly the same speed. It was brilliant.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And he had those little victories. Imagine that over a nine-month period, where you just keep figuring it out, and then it works and then it's successful.

segments.speaker: Ad Tape
segments.text: This is Big Trak, the computer-activated truck from MB Electronics. Program in up to 16 commands and Big Trak will advance, turn, and fire three blasts.

segments.speaker: Ad Tape
segments.text: [FUTURISTIC BLASTING]

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Milton Bradley sold lots of them-- quite a few in Glenside, Pennsylvania, where I grew up. I remember them popping up in friends' houses after Christmas. And those ads were all over TV-- Big Trak rolling across the floor in the suburban living room and delivering an apple to dad.

segments.speaker: Ad Tape
segments.text: Big Trak for your child from MB Electronics. Transporter sold separately.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Sales? Best estimate I was able to find-- $40 million.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: This project, it gave Peter's dad the thing he'd been wanting-- a real success. But people are complicated.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: He was on top of the world. And I know he felt good. He came home and felt good. But that started to sour as he started to realize how much money the company was going to make from this toy.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Because this was his ship that was supposed to come in.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: I think he saw it-- at first, I think he was perfectly happy to be seen as the guy in charge of a project within a corporate framework that's doing well. And as the stakes got higher and the calls from his mom-- every Sunday, his mother would call. And she was never satisfied with where he was in life. I think she would have been really happy if he had been a doctor or a lawyer.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And I think for him, he started to see that he could prove himself with this project. And his self-worth, I think, became really tied up with the success of this project.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Peter's dad was frustrated. He had brought this toy into existence. But in the end, it would be the company's success, not his. The toy was a big hit. But it wasn't going to make his dad rich. Peter would overhear his parents talking in the next room, his dad increasingly unhappy. And, realizing there wasn't going to be any glory for him, he quit the dream job.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: He thought about legal action. But, of course, he couldn't sue Milton Bradley for taking his idea. He was an employee, so the company owned everything he created, which is pretty much how it works at any company. But at some point, Peter's dad talks to a lawyer. And one of the things he says to the lawyer is, hey, the whole idea for Big Trak, I didn't come up with that. It actually came from my son, from Peter, who was not a Milton Bradley employee.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: Then the lawyer says to him, well, a kid can sue a corporation.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: A kid can sue a corporation.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: A kid can sue a corporation. And I know this because my mom had kept diaries her whole life. And I found the diary from the time this was all happening. And she had just noted in there, Steve says, lawyer said, a kid can sue a corporation.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And that is how the lawsuit Peter Ocko, 13-year-old boy, versus the Milton Bradley company came to be. The basis for the lawsuit was that if Peter, the kid, had come up with the initial idea for this multi-million-dollar toy, then he was owed royalties. It could be a lot of money.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I asked Peter if the prospect of being a kid suing a giant corporation felt scary. He said not really, though maybe it should have. He said it felt thrilling, kind of awesome. A big, fancy Boston law firm took their case.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And that firm decides, we're going to take this case on contingency. We actually think this has a really good chance. And you guys won't have to pay anything but the court costs or the Xerox costs. So at this point, my dad is ecstatic. And we're both ecstatic. I'm now playing a really important role in the both of us getting what's due for this idea.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Peter says, looking back, he was just coming into that age where you're really craving some kind of identity. And now he had one, teenage whiz kid.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: I'm just about to go into high school. And, suddenly, I have to take time off from school to go meet with lawyers and give a deposition. And now everybody at my school knows what's going on. And it's really exciting. It's like, I'm at the center of it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Two years went by of preparation, legal back and forth. And, finally, the court date approached. Peter and his dad would take long walks around the block with the dog, both kind of excited by it all, going over the story he would tell in court. And then there was one night, the night Peter's thought about and puzzled over for years.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: We had a dinner conversation that changed my life. I'm not trying to be dramatic. I just-- it's like, I look back at the little pieces that had to move into place for this all to go south. And they're so small.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: To understand what happened, you need to know two things. First was that before bringing the lawsuit, Peter's dad had signed a document making it so that, legally, he no longer had financial responsibility for Peter. This was at the recommendation of the lawyers and made it so that, as far as the jury would be concerned, this would be about Peter, not his dad trying to get money through him-- even though it kind of was. It would also help protect any money they won. That's the first thing you need to know. Here's the other thing.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: My mother and father didn't have a smooth marriage, and that's an understatement. They fought a lot. By the time I was born-- and, certainly, by the time I was a teenager-- they spent a lot of time and energy trying to upset each other.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And if you put that into the soup, along with the fact that my mother now has taken financial control of me and I am the plaintiff in this lawsuit-- we all sit down to dinner soon after that agreement my mom signed. And we're sitting around the table. It's the three of us-- it's a tiny family. We're all sitting there, staring at each other.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And my mom says something to the effect of, well, if you win now, Peter, this money will be yours to control. I'm just your guardian, but it's not the family's. It's really yours. And I think she knew exactly what she was saying. She was absolutely using it to get under my dad's skin.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And my dad was not a drinker. But if he had a beer or two, he would get very grumpy. And he'd had a couple of beers. And he looks at her. And then I-- sort of missing what's going on-- pick it up. And I'm like, yeah, Dad, maybe I'll share the money with you if I win. But it really is-- I am the plaintiff.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And I don't know. I guess if you could see a fuse blow in my father's head, you would have seen it. Because he kind of took a breath. He said, you know, the real truth, Peter, is that I invented Big Trak, not you. I just told you you did it so that we could bring this lawsuit.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And I just remember the bottom falling out. And I don't know. At that moment, to be-- I think I was 14-- and have my dad look at me and say that, it was amazing how easy it was for me to question everything and just feel like everything that had led up to that moment was a bunch of BS. There was something about him staring at me and saying that that I just doubted everything.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Like that moment he remembered, hooking the Simon board up to the motors, when exactly did that happen? Was it really before his dad had started on the project at work? Or was he doing it after his dad began working on Big Trak? Like, maybe what he remembered was him trying to copy the thing his dad was doing.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Also, at this point, this was a family story they had told many times. Maybe it had grown in the telling, and the telling had created its own version in his head. He had all these doubts.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: I'm not a whiz kid. I've been used. I don't know. It's really hard for me to talk about. I guess what I felt at the moment was outrage because I believed that I had done it-- but also, at the same exact moment, tremendous doubt. I remember going later to my mom that night and being like, what's going on? What do you remember?

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And the thing that drove me crazy was, rather than instantly say, like, oh, that's a terrible thing your dad did. Like, he's just in a bad place-- or whatever I would have wished her to say-- instead, she got super vague. And she's like, I don't know what happened.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The court date got closer and closer. His dad had said this confusing and upsetting thing. Peter didn't know what to make of it. And he was all alone with that.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: The hardest part about it was there was no third-party grown-up to weigh in and help me. I couldn't tell the lawyer, hey, listen, my dad said this. What do you think? I had to keep that absolutely to myself and move forward. And my dad did the same thing and my mom did the same thing. And we kind of moved on from that dinner conversation as if nothing had happened.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: I would be in public with my dad. And we would be telling the story of the trial and talking about how excited we were. And he would be smiling with genuine pride at the fact that his kid was the reason he was able to sue the company and we were going to get justice. Like, he was genuinely proud of me in those moments. And then we'd be alone together, and I'd bring up the conversation. He just couldn't talk about it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The trial finally happened. His dad, very invested in it, hated the opposing lawyer, saw him as truly evil. Peter says the whole trial, he wasn't really wondering if they would win. He was looking for clues to what his dad had said and what the truth was.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Eventually, Peter took the stand and swore on the Bible. He says, at that moment, it was the part of him that believed it swearing the oath. He told the story he remembered at that moment in their little workroom at home. His lawyer had him take apart a Simon with a screwdriver on the stand, pull out the circuit board, which seemed to impress the jury.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It's worth noting that the trial was around the time the movie WarGames came out. That's the one where a kid saves the world from nuclear catastrophe because he understands the computers controlling the nuclear weapons better than the adults do. Not surprisingly, the press showed up to the trial. The headline writes itself. "Teenager Sues Milton Bradley."

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: Let's see. "Dedham, Mass-- a 16-year-old high school boy from Brookline claims that the toymaker Milton Bradley company owes him royalties for a robot tank he claims he invented when he was 12."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Oh my god, that's you.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: That's me.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: OK, now read the other headline.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: "Royalties denied to boy who claims toy his idea. A 16-year-old high school student who claimed he invented a toy robot tank at the age of 12 has lost his bid for $2 million in royalties from Milton Bradley company. A Norfolk Superior Court jury decided there was no valid written contract between the toymaker and Peter Ocko, son of Stephen Ocko, who worked until 1978 as a senior game designer for Milton Bradley."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So you guys lost.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: We did.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: What do you remember about that day?

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: Ugh, dark day, literally. It was raining.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: After the verdict came down, they went out the back of the courthouse to avoid the press, the three of them-- mom, dad, and him. There was a phone booth on the way out.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And my dad-- because he couldn't wait-- stepped into one and called his mom. And then he came out, and we all just got in the car. We drove home. And we pulled into the driveway. And we got out of the car. And my dad just kind of walked to the porch. And he sat down on the steps. And he just burst into tears. And I'd never really seen him cry before.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And it was hard. But I do remember feeling a weight lifted-- not just that the trial was over and we didn't have to worry about that, but that all the stuff that had swirled around the truth and the real truth and my dad and me-- that we could just move on.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I'm pretty sure this isn't the goal of the US legal system. But losing this case, it made their lives better. Peter says losing saved them from being the worst versions of themselves, freed them from something bad. And, like three programmable cars, everyone was on a new trajectory. His dad turned left. His mom went right. They got divorced. Peter finished high school and moved away to college.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: His dad began a whole new life after that where he seemed much more at peace. He remarried, got a degree in education, worked with kids and LEGOs, inventing stuff. But that moment, it really broke something. Peter says there was always a hint of competitiveness between him and his dad. It would come up when they talked about where he might go to college. Was his school better than his dad's? Or when he was little when they'd roughhouse-- they both kind of wanted to win. There was a tinge of aggression to it, he says.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And that night at dinner, it was like it flipped some switch between them. Those moments they used to have hanging around in the workroom, happily tinkering together, those were gone. And what was left was a feeling that they were not exactly on the same team anymore.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: It was this kind of lingering sense that we had been thrust into something that made us adversaries and competitors, and we never came out of it. And I came to hate that. I hated that when I would achieve something in my life, like get a new job or whatever, I would hesitate telling my dad because it almost seemed to wound him.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: What we had been through I think had changed both of us and kind of broke something that we never got back. We never got back an empathy.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Peter is pretty sure he knows what the truth is about who came up with the idea for Big Trak. Maybe it was clear at the time. But it was hard to see as a kid-- hard to feel it with confidence, anyway. The truth-- the only thing that really makes sense is-- that Peter had come up with the idea for the toy.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: In the trial, some of his dad's coworkers testified that he had come into work and said as much. And it was a thing that, as a family, they had talked about before the lawsuit, that this little idea Peter had was being turned into an actual toy and how cool that was. But that night at dinner, it was a hard fact for his father to have thrown in his face. And so he said what he said. His dad's way of moving past it was just to keep moving.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Years past. Peter had kids. His dad would come and visit-- really enjoyed being a grandfather.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And I remember thinking, like, this is the dad I remember before that trial. Before all of that started, I remember a kind, sharing, open, curious guy. And it was nice to kind of revisit that. But I would occasionally say to him, do you ever want to talk about this? Because I think about it a lot. And the few times I would bring it up, he would just block. He would just say, I don't. I can't. There's nothing to talk about.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Why do you think he wouldn't just tell you which was the truth?

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: I don't know. Part of me feels that he did something that he was ashamed of and just couldn't talk about that piece of it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The lawsuit did come up one last time, in a very strange way, almost like the universe was trying to put the pieces back together.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: After my dad got cancer, he came out a few times to visit. And one of those times, we had a great visit. And I took him to LAX. And it was back when you could go to the gate with people. And I went to the gate with him. And we were sitting at the gate. And I hear this voice across the room. And it's the attorney from Milton Bradley.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: No way.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And he's standing there with a younger woman-- I'm assuming his daughter. And my dad just tenses up because he sees it, and I see it. And I don't know why. But I just stood up, and I walked over to the guy. And I shake his hand, and I introduce myself. And he's like, oh, Peter, how are you? And I say, oh, I'm fine. My dad's here. And he's like, oh, wonderful.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And he walks with me over to my father. And my father at this point is kind of a deer in the headlights. And I helped my dad stand up. And they shake hands. And I mentioned, I live in Los Angeles. And he says, yeah, my daughter's out here now. And he goes, oh, I always knew you'd be a success, Peter. That's wonderful. And my dad said, yep, I'm really proud of him.

segments.speaker: Peter Ocko
segments.text: And then we just sort of said goodbye. And we sat down. And the attorney got called to first class and went on board. And then we sat there and didn't really say much. And then my dad got called on to coach, and off he went. And that was one of the last times I saw him.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The earliest known version of the Humpty Dumpty rhyme, it's not the same as the one you know. It may have been a riddle about an egg, or it may have been a poem about a person. It went like this.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: "Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall. Humpty Dumpty had a great fall. Four-score men and four-score more could not make Humpty Dumpty where he was before--" which I read differently from the one we know. You can put a broken thing back together. It's just going to be different.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: David Kestenbaum is our senior editor. Coming up, a man-- not an egg-- falls off a very high wall. And he does not look around for either king's horses or king's men. Imagine that. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today's program, "All the King's Horses"-- about things broken so badly, they cannot be put back together. We've arrived at act two of our program.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act two, The 95. This next story is about somebody examining something very broken, something documented in a list assembled by the Committee to Protect Journalists, of journalists who've been killed in the Israel-Hamas war. It's the largest number of journalists who've died in any conflict since they started counting.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The list gives each person's name, where they worked, circumstances of their death-- sometimes a few more details, but often, that's all. Reporter Dana Ballout has been reading about the people on the list, watching their work, talking to their colleagues, trying to piece together who they were and what was lost when they died. Here she is.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: I first started noticing the journalists dying on Instagram. I'm a journalist. I'm Arab. And I've reported on war. A big part of my community is other Arab journalists who do the same thing. And when someone dies, news travels fast.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Recently, I pulled up the list that the Committee to Protect Journalists has been keeping and looked at it for the first time. There are 95 journalists and media workers on it as of today. Almost everyone on it is Palestinian. Scrolling through, I started to get angry. These were the people carrying the burden of documenting this whole war.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Israel is not allowing foreign journalists into Gaza, except on rare occasions with military escorts. These people's names are being buried in a giant list that keeps growing. What I want to do is lift some of them off the list for a moment and give you a glimpse of who they were and the work they made.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: I'll start with Sari Mansour. Sari was the director of Al Quds News Network. And he posted a 22-second video on November 18 that was a report from the war, but it also gave me a picture into his marriage.

segments.speaker: Sari Mansour
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Sari's wearing his press vest and looks exhausted. He's explaining that cell service and the internet keep getting cut off and it's often impossible to text or call anyone, including his wife. So they've resorted to using handwritten letters to communicate while he's out reporting, sending them back and forth with neighbors or colleagues.

segments.speaker: Sari Mansour
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: He ends the video with a picture of one of these letters from his wife. In it, she writes, "Me and the kids stayed up waiting for you until the morning, and you didn't come home. We were really sad. I kept telling the kids, look, he's coming. But you didn't show up. May God forgive you.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Come home tomorrow and eat with us. Do you want me to make you kebab or maybe kabseh? Bring your friends with you. It's OK. And give Aziz the battery to charge. What do you think about me sending you handwritten letters with messenger pigeons from now on? Ha, ha, ha. I'm just kidding. I want to curse at you, but we're living in a war. Too bad. OK, I love you. Bye."

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: A few hours after he shared that letter, Sari and his coworker, Hassouneh Salim, were at Sari's home when they were killed by an Israeli airstrike that hit his house. His wife and kids, who weren't there, survived.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Gaza's tiny, and the journalist community is really close. Reading the list, you can see all the connections between people, like with Ibrahim Lafi. Ibrahim was a photo journalist, one of the first journalists to die. He was killed while reporting on October 7. He was just 21, still new to journalism.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: On his Instagram, you can see that in his posts just a few years ago, he was still practicing his photography, taking pictures of coffee cups and flowers. Then he started doing beautiful portraits and action shots. You can really feel him starting to become a journalist.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Clicking around on Instagram, I found a tribute post about Ibrahim from his coworker, Roshdi Serraj. In this photo, Ibrahim's staring intently at the back of a camera, his face lit up by the light from the viewfinder. He looks so young. The caption reads, "My assistant is gone. Ibrahim is gone."

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Roshdi himself was a beloved journalist and filmmaker. And I know that because he's also on the list. He was killed just two weeks after Ibrahim. I read the tribute post to him too. I saw this over and over again, journalists posting tributes, who were then killed themselves soon after. And a tribute goes up for them. And then the pattern continues.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Something else I saw over and over on the list, journalists-- later in the war-- who'd become aware that they could be making their last reports. They'd say it at the beginning of their videos. And those were the hardest to watch, especially when it was true.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: One video like that was posted by Ayat Khadoura. Ayat was a freelance journalist and video blogger. Her videos before the war covered a wide range, from what I can tell-- interviews about women in politics. She even appeared in a commercial for ketchup-flavored chips. She clearly liked being in front of the camera.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Once the war started, Ayat pivoted to covering bombings and food shortages. On November 20, she posted a video report from her home. You can hear the airstrikes hitting very close to where she is. It's scary.

segments.speaker: Ayat Khadoura
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: She's saying, this is likely my last video. Today the occupation forces dropped phosphorus bombs on Beit Lehia area and frightening sound bombs. They dropped letters from the sky ordering everyone to evacuate. Everyone ran into the streets in the craziest way. No one knows where to go.

segments.speaker: Ayat Khadoura
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: My family and I are split up. Myself and a few others are still at home, but everyone else has evacuated. They don't know where they're going. The situation is so scary. What's happening is so tough, and may God mercy on us.

segments.speaker: Ayat Khadoura
segments.text: [SPEAKING ARABIC]

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: And then she begins to cry and the video stops. She was killed later that day.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Targeting journalists, in case you didn't know, is a war crime. So far, the Committee to Protect Journalists has found that three of the journalists on the list were explicitly targeted by the IDF, the Israeli military. Investigations by the Washington Post and Reuters, Human Rights Watch, and the United Nations have also raised serious questions in these three cases. And the Committee to Protect Journalists is investigating 10 other killings.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: When we reached out to the IDF for comment, they said, quote, "The IDF has never and will never deliberately target journalists." That's the answer they always give in these situations.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Meanwhile, dozens of seasoned reporters have fled Gaza-- journalists who worked for Al Jazeera, the BBC, the New York Times, the Washington Post, Reuters, Agence France Presse. So many media offices were demolished in Israeli airstrikes that the Committee to Protect Journalists stopped counting. It's not just individual lives that have been destroyed. It's an entire infrastructure.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: The name on the list that was hardest for me to look at was Issam Abdallah because I'd crossed paths with him once. Issam was a Lebanese journalist, a video journalist for Reuters for many, many years. He had just won an award for coverage of Ukraine. I'm Lebanese and still report there sometimes. And I'd worked with Issam a couple of summers ago.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: He helped me film a sort of random story in Beirut. I was interviewing this entrepreneur who had started a sperm-freezing company after an accident where he spilled a tray of hot coffee on his private area, burning himself. I know-- ridiculous. It was a really silly shoot.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Right after we said cut and started to wrap, Issam started this whole bit about being in his late 30s, reconsidering his own sperm quality, and everything he now realized he was doing to hurt it. And no one could stop laughing. It was a really good day. That felt good to remember-- and to remember him that way.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: Issam was killed by the IDF on October 13. His death was one of the three that the Committee to Protect Journalists has identified as a targeted killing. He was fired upon by an Israeli tank while standing in an empty field on the Lebanon-Israel border with a small group of other journalists. Everyone was wearing press vests with cameras out. They were covering the Hezbollah part of this war. A few other journalists were injured in the attack, which was captured on video.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: The IDF says they were responding to firing from Hezbollah, not targeting the journalists. But multiple investigations, including by Reuters, the United Nations, Amnesty International, and the AFP found no evidence of any firing from the location of the journalist before the IDF shot at them. The journalists in the group and video footage confirmed that there was no military activity near them.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: I'd only met Issam once, barely knew him, but it affected me so much when he died. I know that he understood the risks of his job. But somehow, it still felt so random and unfair that he would be struck down like that, following the rules, wearing his press vest and helmet in a pack of reporters on a sunny day in an open field. I find myself thinking about him all the time.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: His last Instagram post was commemorating another journalist, this iconic reporter, Shireen Abu Akleh, who'd been killed by the IDF. When I first saw that post in October, I thought, how ironic. Because a week later, Issam also was killed by the IDF. But then after spending time reading the list, I realized how common this had become.

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: I still haven't finished going through the list and looking up the people on it. I keep finding things that stick with me, like the funny way this one radio host would cut off a caller who was rambling on for too long, a tweet from reporter Ola Atallah that quoted Sylvia Plath. It read, "What ceremony of words can patch the havoc?"

segments.speaker: Dana Ballout
segments.text: I'm going to keep going down the list even though this radio story is over now, just for myself, my own way of bearing witness, which is, in the end, all that these journalists were trying to do.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Reporter Dana Ballou is journalist and documentary filmmaker. Her story was produced by Diane Wu.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: ["RECORDING 801" BY LINA MAKOUL]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This song is by Lina Makoul, a Palestinian musician it's called "Recording 801."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act 3, A Great Fall. OK, so there are lots of ways to break something. And skateboarding is a pretty good one. David Kestenbaum-- who, of course, you heard earlier in the show-- has been obsessed with this one short video of a skateboarder that he keeps watching over and over.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The skateboarder stands at the top of a ramp. The wall of the ramp goes straight down at first, then curves into a flat section, then up again on the other side. It's like an enormous U. You could easily break something from that height. He leans forward. It's 13 and 1/2 feet down. One other number you should know-- 52. That's how old he is in this video-- 52 years old. It's Tony Hawk trying to land a trick that he used to do all the time when he was younger.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: He goes down the ramp, up the other side, spins in the air and--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [CRASH]

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: --falls onto his knees. He's wearing pads, slides to the bottom, then climbs the stairs to try again. But same thing.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [CRASH]

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I was never a skateboard kid-- they were too cool for me. I know Tony Hawk is the most famous skateboarder in the world, but I've only gotten into him now that he's over 50. On social media, he writes these funny little scenes from his life, like this one.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Kid at skate park. Are you Tony Hawk? Me-- I am. Him-- no, you're not. OK, I'm not. But are you, for real? I am, for real. I thought you'd look younger. Me too.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So the trick he was trying to do in this video, it's called an Ollie 540. Basically, you go down the ramp, up the other side of the U, then down again-- that a couple times until you get enough height. Then, through some kind of magic, at, like, 15 feet in the air, you spin one and a half times with the board turning underneath you but without grabbing the board. You don't touch it with your hands. Like, you and the board are just rotating it exactly the same speed. And then somehow, you try to land on your skateboard without breaking any bones.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [CRASH]

segments.speaker: Tony Hawk
segments.text: Hip.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Hip, I think he says there. He's written that the trick has gotten scarier as he's gotten older, just committing to the landing at the end. He wrote, "My willingness to slam unexpectedly into the flat bottom has waned greatly over the last decade."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: One of the things I like about this video is it's basically a collection of failures over and over. It's edited so you can't see how many tries, but it's a lot. He looks tired and just so human. After one fall, he sits there on the ground, looks up, and swears.

segments.speaker: Tony Hawk
segments.text: Fuck.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The next attempt literally goes sideways. He slides out the end of the ramp and takes out a camera there that's filming.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [CRASH]

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [CLATTERING]

segments.speaker: Tony Hawk
segments.text: Sorry. I broke everything.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Shy grin, he checks to see if his finger is OK. Cut to Tony Hawk at the top of the ramp again. Deep breath, skateboard over the void again. Plunges down, up the other side, down, up into the air, around--

segments.speaker: Tony Hawk
segments.text: Woo-hoo!

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: --and he lands it. Lets the board go flying, covers his face with his hands, drops to his knees and says this.

segments.speaker: Tony Hawk
segments.text: I'm kind of sad.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: "I'm kind of sad," he says. One of the film crew fist bumps him.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Did it! So sick, dude.

segments.speaker: Tony Hawk
segments.text: [INAUDIBLE].

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Perfect.

segments.speaker: Tony Hawk
segments.text: I'm a little sad.

segments.speaker: Tony Hawk
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: That was the last one.

segments.speaker: Tony Hawk
segments.text: Yeah. I never had much finality to anything, but that definitely was the last one I'll ever do. Fuck it. Happy I made it.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: It was literally perfect.

segments.speaker: Tony Hawk
segments.text: Thanks, you guys, for hanging in there with me.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The title of the video when it got posted was "Tony Hawk lands his last ever Ollie 540, aged 52."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I tear up every time I watch this-- in part, because we're basically the same age. He's one year older. Something happens when you're around 50. You can't do things you used to do because stuff hurts. I used to love to run, really love it. I can't anymore-- four knee surgeries. And walking around, I notice things I didn't used to. So many people with little hitches in their steps, working around some bit of pain in a knee, a hip.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I reached out to Tony Hawk back when the video came out. I wanted to talk about it. Apparently, he did not-- declined my interview request. So this is going to be a short story. I'll just say this.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: A friend told me recently about a doctor who'd gone to work in a small town, ended up treating a lot of older people. And he noticed that the way it would go is that, first, one thing would go wrong. You'd fix it. Then a different thing would go wrong. You'd fix that. Then two things would go wrong at once and then another. Eventually, enough things would break that that's the end. He also said something else. That's the good version, he said. That's the one you want, the one where you get to keep going long enough that all the parts break.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: David Kestenbaum is still making radio stories at 54. Tony Hawk-- a year after that video-- broke his femur. But after surgeries, he's still skateboarding.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass

You know, he has started saying my name so much-- like, at the end of every sentence he says. I told him, Torey people do not usually talk to each other this way. He said--

segments.speaker: Uncle Bennett
segments.text: Oh, it happens all the time, Ira.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I'm Ira Glass, back next week with more stories of This American Life.
